l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 5
s: The Amorite and Canaanite kings west of the Jordan lose heart upon hearing that the LORD dried up the Jordan for the children of Israel. The LORD tells Joshua to make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel again, because those born in the wilderness had not been circumcised while the generation that left Egypt had died there for not listening to the LORD. After the people heal, the LORD declares that he has rolled away the reproach of Egypt, and the place is named Gilgal. The Israelites keep the Passover in the plains of Jericho, eat the produce of the land, and the manna ceases. Near Jericho, Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword who identifies himself as commander of the LORD's army and tells Joshua to take off his sandals because the place is holy.

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 5
s: Joshua makes flint knives at the LORD's command and circumcises the sons of Israel at the hill of the foreskins. Near Jericho he meets a man with a drawn sword, asks whether he is for Israel or its enemies, then falls on his face and worships, asks what his lord says to his servant, and obeys the order to take off his sandals.

l: LORD, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 5
s: The LORD dried up the Jordan for Israel's crossing, which melted the hearts of the Canaanite and Amorite kings. He commands Joshua to circumcise the sons of Israel again, declares that he has rolled away the reproach of Egypt, and is recalled as having sworn that the disobedient exodus generation would not see the promised land. The manna ceases once the people eat the produce of the land.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 5
s: The children of Israel are circumcised at the LORD's command, stay in camp until healed, and camp at Gilgal. They keep the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month in the plains of Jericho, eat unleavened cakes and parched grain of the land, and no longer receive manna, eating the fruit of Canaan that year.

l: Gilgal, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 5
s: Gilgal is the place where the Israelites encamp, and it receives its name after the LORD says he has rolled away the reproach of Egypt from them. The name is said to endure to the time of writing.

l: Jericho, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 5
s: The Israelites keep the Passover in the plains of Jericho. Joshua is by Jericho when he sees the man with the drawn sword.

l: circumcision, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 5
s: The LORD commands that the sons of Israel be circumcised a second time with flint knives, and Joshua carries it out. It was needed because those born in the wilderness along the way had not been circumcised, and the people stayed in camp until healed. It is linked to the LORD's rolling away the reproach of Egypt.

l: generation of the exodus (men of war who came out of Egypt), The Book of Joshua, Chapter 5
s: All the males and men of war who came out of Egypt had been circumcised but died in the wilderness after forty years of walking. They were consumed because they did not listen to the LORD's voice, and the LORD swore they would not see the land promised to their fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey. Their children were raised up in their place.

l: commander of the LORD's army, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 5
s: A man stands before Joshua near Jericho with his sword drawn and answers Joshua's question with "No," saying he has come as commander of the LORD's army. Joshua worships him, and he tells Joshua to take off his sandals because the place where he stands is holy.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 6
s: Jericho is tightly shut against the children of Israel when the LORD tells Joshua he has given the city into his hand and prescribes a march: armed men and seven priests with ram's horn trumpets circle it once daily for six days, then seven times on the seventh. Joshua commands silence until the day to shout, and the people obey. On the seventh day, at Joshua's command and the priests' trumpet blast, the people shout, the wall falls flat, and Israel takes the city. Everything living in it is destroyed with the sword and the city is burned, while the silver, gold, bronze and iron go into the LORD's treasury. Rahab the prostitute and her household are spared because she hid the messengers, and Joshua pronounces a curse on anyone who rebuilds Jericho, so that the LORD is with Joshua and his fame spreads.

l: Jericho, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 6
s: Jericho is tightly shut up, with no one going in or out, because of the children of Israel. The LORD gives it into Joshua's hand, its wall falls flat after the shout, and it is taken, utterly destroyed and burned. Joshua curses anyone who rebuilds it, saying the man will lose his firstborn when laying its foundation and his youngest son when setting up its gates.

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 6
s: Joshua receives the LORD's battle plan for Jericho, directs the priests and people to carry it out, and commands silence until the day of the shout. He gives the shout command on the seventh day, instructs that the city be devoted and its metals go to the treasury, sends the two spies to bring Rahab out, and saves her household alive. He pronounces a curse on whoever rebuilds Jericho, and the LORD is with him so that his fame spreads through the land.

l: LORD, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 6
s: The LORD tells Joshua he has given Jericho, its king and its mighty men into his hand, and prescribes the marching and trumpet procedure that will bring the wall down. The city is devoted to him, and the silver, gold, bronze and iron are declared holy to him and go into his treasury. He is with Joshua, whose fame spreads in all the land.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 6
s: The children of Israel are the reason Jericho is tightly shut up. Their camp is warned not to take any devoted thing lest it become accursed and troubled. Rahab and her family are brought out and set outside the camp of Israel, and Rahab lives in the middle of Israel to this day.

l: Rahab, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 6
s: Rahab the prostitute is exempted from the devotion to destruction because she hid the messengers Joshua sent. The two spies go into her house and bring out Rahab with her father, mother, brothers, relatives and all she had, as they had sworn to her. Joshua saves her and her father's household alive, and she lives in the middle of Israel to this day.

l: priests (seven priests), The Book of Joshua, Chapter 6
s: Seven priests bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD and blow them as they march around Jericho. They do this once a day for six days and seven times on the seventh day. Their trumpet blast at the seventh circuit precedes Joshua's command to shout.

l: ark of the covenant, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 6
s: The ark of the LORD's covenant is carried by the priests in the procession around Jericho, with armed men going before the priests and a rear guard after the ark. It circles the city once daily for six days and seven times on the seventh day, returning to the camp each day.

l: Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 6
s: Joshua's people march around Jericho as commanded and stay silent until he tells them to shout. On the seventh day they shout with a great shout at the trumpet sound, go up into the city straight ahead, take it, and destroy all that is in it with the sword. They are warned against taking devoted things, and the metals go into the LORD's treasury.

l: wall of Jericho, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 6
s: The LORD says the city wall will fall down flat when the people shout at the long ram's horn blast. When the people shout on the seventh day, the wall falls down flat, and the people go up into the city, each man straight in front of him.

l: destruction of Jericho, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 6
s: After the wall falls, the people utterly destroy everything in the city with the sword: man and woman, young and old, ox, sheep and donkey. The city and all in it are burned, except that the silver, gold, bronze and iron go into the treasury of the LORD's house. Only Rahab and her household are spared.

l: march around Jericho, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 6
s: On six days the armed men, seven priests with trumpets and the ark circle the city once daily, then return to camp, while the people stay silent. On the seventh day they rise early and circle seven times, and at the final blast Joshua commands the shout. The march ends with the wall falling and the city being taken.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 7
s: Achan, of the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things from Jericho, so the LORD's anger burned against Israel. Israel's attack on Ai with about three thousand men failed, with thirty-six killed, and Joshua and the elders mourned before the LORD's ark. The LORD told Joshua that Israel had become devoted for destruction and would not stand before its enemies until the devoted things were removed, and he directed a selection by tribe, family, household, and man that singled out Achan. Achan confessed to taking a Babylonian robe, two hundred shekels of silver, and a fifty-shekel wedge of gold hidden in his tent; Joshua and all Israel then took him, his family, his possessions, and the stolen goods to the valley of Achor, stoned and burned them, and raised a heap of stones, after which the LORD turned from his anger.

l: Achan, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 7
s: Achan, son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things. He was singled out by the LORD's selection and confessed that he coveted and took a Babylonian robe, two hundred shekels of silver, and a fifty-shekel wedge of gold, hiding them in his tent. He was stoned and burned with his sons, daughters, livestock, tent, and all he had in the valley of Achor.

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 7
s: Joshua sent men to spy out Ai, then tore his clothes and lay on his face before the LORD's ark until evening after the defeat, lamenting to the LORD. Following the LORD's instructions, he sanctified the people, conducted the selection that identified Achan, urged him to confess, and led Israel in carrying out the judgment on him.

l: LORD, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 7
s: The LORD's anger burned against Israel because of the trespass in the devoted things. He told Joshua to get up, explained that Israel had sinned and would not stand before its enemies until the devoted things were removed, and directed the selection that exposed Achan. After the judgment he turned from the fierceness of his anger.

l: Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 7
s: Israel, through Achan's trespass, became devoted for destruction and fled before the men of Ai, their hearts melting like water. They were sanctified and brought near by tribe, family, household, and man, then all Israel took part in stoning and burning Achan and his household and raised a heap of stones over him.

l: Ai, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 7
s: Ai, beside Beth Aven on the east side of Bethel, was spied out by Joshua's men, who judged its people few. The men of Ai defeated the roughly three thousand Israelites who attacked, striking about thirty-six and chasing them from the gate to Shebarim and down the descent.

l: devoted things (Jericho's silver, gold, bronze, iron), The Book of Joshua, Chapter 7
s: The devoted things were taken in part by Achan, which was a trespass and a breach of the LORD's covenant. The LORD said Israel had become devoted for destruction and he would not be with them unless the devoted things were destroyed from among them. The robe, silver, and gold were found hidden in Achan's tent and laid before the LORD.

l: valley of Achor, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 7
s: The valley of Achor is where Israel brought Achan, his family, his possessions, and the stolen goods to be stoned and burned. A great heap of stones was raised over him there, and the place received its name, which it still bears to this day.

l: Achan's sin and judgment, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 7
s: Achan's covetous taking of devoted plunder and hiding it in his tent brought the LORD's anger on all Israel. He was exposed by a selection through tribe, family, and household, confessed, and the hidden goods were recovered. He and all that he had were stoned and burned in the valley of Achor, and the LORD turned from his anger.

l: defeat at Ai, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 7
s: After spies advised sending only two or three thousand men, about three thousand went up against Ai and fled, with about thirty-six killed. The people's hearts melted, and Joshua and the elders mourned. The LORD explained the defeat as the result of the devoted thing among Israel.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 8
s: The LORD tells Joshua not to fear and instructs him to take all the warriors to Ai, giving it into his hand and permitting Israel to keep its goods and livestock. Joshua sends thirty thousand men to lie in ambush behind the city, then draws the men of Ai out by feigning defeat. When Joshua stretches out his javelin, the ambush takes and burns the city, and Israel turns back and kills the men of Ai caught in the middle, killing twelve thousand in all, capturing the king alive, and later hanging him on a tree. Joshua burns Ai into a permanent heap and Israel takes only the livestock and goods. Joshua then builds an altar of uncut stones on Mount Ebal, writes a copy of Moses' law on stones, and reads all the words of the law, blessing and curse, to all Israel at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 8
s: Joshua receives the LORD's instruction to take all the warriors up to Ai, plans the ambush, and leads the feigned retreat that draws the men of Ai out of the city. At the LORD's command he stretches out his javelin toward Ai and does not draw back his hand until all its inhabitants are destroyed. He then burns Ai, hangs its king, builds an altar on Mount Ebal, writes the law on stones, and reads all its words to the assembly.

l: LORD, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 8
s: The LORD tells Joshua not to be afraid, declares that he has given Ai and its king into Joshua's hand, and commands the ambush and the keeping of the spoil. He directs Joshua to stretch out the javelin toward Ai, and Israel acts throughout according to his word.

l: Ai, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 8
s: Ai is attacked by Israel after its earlier victory, and its city is left open when every man in Ai and Bethel pursues Israel. It is taken by the ambush, set on fire, struck with the sword, and made a heap and desolation forever.

l: king of Ai, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 8
s: The king of Ai hurries out early with all his people to battle Israel, not knowing of the ambush behind the city. He is captured alive and brought to Joshua, hanged on a tree until evening, and his body is thrown at the city gate and covered with a great heap of stones that remains to this day.

l: men of Ai, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 8
s: The men of Ai go out against Israel and pursue the fleeing Israelites away from their city, believing it is like the first time. They see the city's smoke behind them, are trapped between Israel's forces, and are struck down so that none remain or escape.

l: Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 8
s: Israel, under Joshua, feigns defeat before Ai, then turns back when the city's smoke rises and kills the men of Ai. They take only the livestock and goods of the city as the LORD commanded. All Israel, including elders, officers, judges, women, little ones, and foreigners, later assembles at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal to hear the law.

l: ambush force (Joshua's men at Ai), The Book of Joshua, Chapter 8
s: Thirty thousand mighty men of valor are sent out by night to lie in ambush behind the city, between Bethel and Ai on the west side; the text also says Joshua set about five thousand men in ambush there. When Joshua stretches out his javelin, they rise quickly, enter the city, take it, and set it on fire.

l: Mount Ebal, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 8
s: Mount Ebal is where Joshua builds an altar to the LORD and writes a copy of Moses' law on stones. Half of the people stand in front of it, and half in front of Mount Gerizim, for the blessing and the reading of the law.

l: altar (Joshua's altar on Mount Ebal), The Book of Joshua, Chapter 8
s: Joshua builds the altar to the LORD, the God of Israel, of uncut stones on which no one had lifted up any iron, as Moses commanded and as written in the book of the law. Israel offers burnt offerings and sacrifices peace offerings on it.

l: book of the law of Moses, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 8
s: The altar is built according to what Moses commanded, as written in the book of the law of Moses. Joshua writes a copy of Moses' law on stones before the children of Israel and reads all its words, the blessing and the curse, omitting nothing, before the whole assembly.

l: destruction of Ai, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 8
s: Ai is destroyed through the ambush and the feigned retreat, with twelve thousand men and women falling that day, and Joshua does not draw back his hand until all its inhabitants are utterly destroyed. The city is burned and made a permanent heap and desolation, its livestock and goods are taken as spoil, and its king is hanged and buried under stones at the gate.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 9
s: Kings west of the Jordan hear of Israel's victories and gather to fight Joshua and Israel. The inhabitants of Gibeon instead resort to a ruse, disguising themselves as ambassadors from a far country with old sacks, patched sandals, and moldy bread, and ask Joshua for a covenant. Joshua and the princes of the congregation make peace and swear an oath to them without asking counsel from the LORD. Three days later Israel learns the Gibeonites are neighbors living among them, but the princes refuse to let the congregation strike them because of the oath. Joshua curses the Gibeonites and makes them wood cutters and drawers of water for the congregation and the LORD's altar.

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 9
s: Joshua receives the disguised Gibeonites at Gilgal, questions them, and makes peace and a covenant with them to let them live. After learning of the deception he confronts them, pronounces them cursed, and appoints them wood cutters and drawers of water for the congregation and the LORD's altar, sparing them from being killed.

l: Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 9
s: The men of Israel question the Gibeonites' claim, sample their provisions, and do not ask counsel from the LORD. After discovering the ruse, the congregation murmurs against the princes but does not strike the Gibeonites because of the oath sworn by the LORD.

l: Gibeonites, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 9
s: The inhabitants of Gibeon, whose cities are Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath Jearim, fear for their lives after hearing what Joshua did to Jericho and Ai and trick Israel into a covenant. When exposed, they explain they knew of the LORD's command to Moses to destroy the land's inhabitants, submit to Joshua's judgment, and are made wood cutters and drawers of water.

l: princes of the congregation, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 9
s: The princes swear an oath to the Gibeonites by the LORD, the God of Israel. When the congregation murmurs, they insist the oath must be honored lest wrath fall on Israel, and they decree that the Gibeonites live as wood cutters and drawers of water.

l: LORD, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 9
s: The LORD is the name invoked by the Gibeonites as the reason for their supposed journey, and his fame in Egypt and against Sihon and Og is cited. The Israelites do not ask counsel from his mouth, and the oath is sworn by him, which binds Israel; the Gibeonites also say he commanded Moses to give Israel the land and destroy its inhabitants.

l: covenant with the Gibeonites, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 9
s: Joshua makes peace and a covenant with the Gibeonites to let them live, and the princes of the congregation swear to it. Though its basis proves false, the oath is honored out of fear of wrath, and the Gibeonites are not killed.

l: Gibeonite deception, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 9
s: The Gibeonites disguise themselves with old sacks, torn wineskins, patched sandals, old garments, and dry moldy bread, claiming to come from a far country. It succeeds, and the covenant is made, but three days later Israel learns they live nearby, and Joshua asks why they deceived him.

l: wood cutters and drawers of water, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 9
s: This is the servile role assigned to the Gibeonites by the princes and then by Joshua, who makes them serve the congregation and the LORD's altar in the place he should choose. It is presented as a lasting condition that continues to this day, in place of killing them.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 10
s: Adoni-Zedek, king of Jerusalem, alarmed that Gibeon had made peace with Israel, rallies four other Amorite kings (of Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon) to attack Gibeon. The Gibeonites appeal to Joshua, who marches from Gilgal overnight, and the LORD routs the coalition at Gibeon, killing many with great hailstones, while the sun and moon stand still at Joshua's command. The five kings hide in a cave at Makkedah, are later brought out, humiliated by Israel's commanders, killed, hanged, and thrown back into the cave. Joshua then takes Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, and Debir, defeating Horam king of Gezer along the way, and the chapter summarizes that he struck the whole land from Kadesh Barnea to Gaza and Goshen to Gibeon before returning to Gilgal.

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 10
s: Joshua marched all night from Gilgal to relieve Gibeon, was assured by the LORD of victory, and asked the sun and moon to stand still during the battle. He had the five kings killed and hanged, then took Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, and Debir, utterly destroying them, and returned to Gilgal.

l: Adoni-Zedek, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 10
s: Adoni-Zedek, king of Jerusalem, feared Israel after hearing of the fall of Ai and Jericho and Gibeon's peace with Israel. He summoned the kings of Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon to attack Gibeon, and he was among the five kings who hid in the cave at Makkedah and were later killed.

l: five Amorite kings, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 10
s: The kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon gathered their armies and besieged Gibeon, but were routed by Israel and the LORD. They hid in the cave at Makkedah, were brought out, had Israel's commanders place their feet on their necks, were struck down and hanged on five trees until evening, and were thrown into the cave.

l: LORD, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 10
s: The LORD told Joshua not to fear because he had delivered the enemy into his hands, confused the Amorites, and hurled great stones from the sky on them. He listened to the voice of a man when the sun stood still, and is said to have fought for Israel and to have commanded the utter destruction of all that breathed.

l: Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 10
s: Israel, led by Joshua, defeated the Amorite coalition at Gibeon and pursued it, then returned in peace to Joshua at Makkedah with none speaking against them. Israel went on to conquer the cities of the south and the surrounding land, then returned to the camp at Gilgal.

l: Gibeon, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 10
s: Gibeon is described as a great city, like one of the royal cities, greater than Ai, with mighty men. It was besieged by the five Amorite kings because of its peace with Israel, and was relieved when Joshua came to its aid.

l: Gibeonites, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 10
s: The men of Gibeon, having made peace with Israel, sent to Joshua at Gilgal begging him not to abandon his servants and to come quickly to save them. Their appeal brought Joshua and his army to their rescue.

l: Makkedah, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 10
s: Makkedah was where the pursuit reached, and the five kings hid in a cave there. Joshua later took the city on that day, struck it and its king with the sword, and left no one remaining.

l: cave at Makkedah, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 10
s: The five kings hid in this cave, and Joshua had large stones rolled over its entrance and guards set by it. After the kings were killed, their bodies were thrown back into the cave and great stones were laid on its mouth, which remain to this day.

l: hailstones, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 10
s: At the descent of Beth Horon, the LORD hurled great stones from the sky on the fleeing Amorites as far as Azekah. More died from the hailstones than from the Israelites' swords.

l: sun and moon standing still, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 10
s: Joshua commanded the sun to stand still over Gibeon and the moon in the valley of Aijalon, and they stayed until the nation avenged itself on its enemies. The text cites the book of Jashar and says the sun stayed in mid-sky about a whole day, with no day like it before or after.

l: Battle of Gibeon, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 10
s: After a night march from Gilgal, Joshua surprised the five Amorite kings' armies at Gibeon, where the LORD confused them and Israel killed many. The rout continued via Beth Horon to Azekah and Makkedah, aided by hailstones and the standing still of the sun and moon.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 11
s: Jabin king of Hazor summons a coalition of northern kings, who gather with a vast army, horses and chariots at the waters of Merom to fight Israel. The LORD tells Joshua not to fear and to hamstring their horses and burn their chariots; Joshua attacks suddenly, routs them as far as great Sidon, and leaves none remaining. Joshua then takes Hazor, kills its king and all inhabitants, and burns it, and goes on to capture and utterly destroy the other cities as Moses commanded, though only Hazor is burned. Joshua makes war a long time, takes the whole land, and removes the Anakim except in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod, and no city but Gibeon of the Hivites makes peace because the LORD hardened their hearts. Joshua gives the land to Israel as an inheritance by tribal divisions, and the land has rest from war.

l: Jabin, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 11
s: Jabin king of Hazor, on hearing of Israel's conquests, sends to other kings to form a coalition against Israel. He is struck down with the sword when Joshua takes Hazor.

l: Hazor, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 11
s: Hazor is described as formerly the head of all those kingdoms. Joshua takes it, kills its king and all its people, and burns it, the only city on a mound that Israel burned.

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 11
s: Joshua attacks the coalition suddenly at Merom, hamstrings the horses and burns the chariots as the LORD told him, and takes Hazor. He wages war a long time, captures the whole land, destroys the Anakim, leaves nothing undone of what the LORD commanded Moses, and gives the land to Israel by tribal divisions.

l: Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 11
s: Israel, under Joshua, defeats the northern coalition, strikes the cities with the sword, and takes their plunder and livestock. Israel receives the land as an inheritance by tribes, and the land rests from war.

l: LORD, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 11
s: The LORD tells Joshua not to fear and promises to deliver the enemy slain before Israel, and he commands the hamstringing of horses and burning of chariots. He delivers them into Israel's hand and hardens the hearts of the peoples so that they come to battle and are utterly destroyed, as he commanded Moses.

l: Moses, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 11
s: Moses, called the servant of the LORD, is the source of the command that Joshua carried out in utterly destroying the cities and inhabitants. He commanded Joshua as the LORD commanded him, and the land is taken according to what the LORD spoke to him.

l: northern coalition of kings, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 11
s: Jabin summons Jobab of Madon and the kings of Shimron and Achshaph, along with kings of the north, hill country, Arabah, lowland and Dor, and various peoples including Canaanites, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites and Hivites. They muster a multitude like the sand of the seashore with many horses and chariots, and are routed and destroyed by Israel.

l: waters of Merom, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 11
s: The waters of Merom are where all the allied kings meet and encamp together to fight Israel. Joshua attacks them there suddenly.

l: Battle of Merom, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 11
s: Joshua and all the warriors attack the encamped coalition at the waters of Merom, and the LORD delivers them into Israel's hand. Israel chases them to great Sidon, Misrephoth Maim and the valley of Mizpah, leaving none remaining, and then hamstrings the horses and burns the chariots.

l: Canaanite land conquered by Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 11
s: Joshua captures all the land: the hill country, the South, the land of Goshen, the lowland, the Arabah, and the hill country and lowland of Israel, from Mount Halak up to Seir to Baal Gad under Hermon. He gives it as an inheritance to Israel by tribes, and it has rest from war.

l: Anakim, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 11
s: Joshua cuts off the Anakim from the hill country, including Hebron, Debir, Anab, and the hill country of Judah and Israel, and utterly destroys them with their cities. Only in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod do some remain.

l: utter destruction of the inhabitants, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 11
s: Israel strikes every person in Hazor and the other captured cities with the sword, leaving none who breathed, while taking the plunder and livestock. The text presents this as commanded by the LORD through Moses, and as the purpose of the LORD hardening the peoples' hearts so they would receive no favor.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 12
s: Chapter 12 lists the kings defeated by the children of Israel. East of the Jordan, from the valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon, Moses and the children of Israel struck Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon, and Og king of Bashan, of the remnant of the Rephaim. Moses gave their land to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. West of the Jordan, from Baal Gad to Mount Halak, Joshua and the children of Israel struck the kings of the land, and Joshua gave that land to the tribes of Israel according to their divisions. The chapter names the cities of the kings, from Jericho to Tirzah, and totals them at thirty-one.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 12
s: The children of Israel struck the kings east of the Jordan with Moses and possessed their land from the valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon. They then struck the thirty-one kings west of the Jordan with Joshua, and the land was given to the tribes of Israel as a possession.

l: Moses, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 12
s: Moses, called the servant of the LORD, struck Sihon and Og together with the children of Israel. He gave their land east of the Jordan as a possession to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh.

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 12
s: Joshua and the children of Israel struck the kings west of the Jordan, from Baal Gad in the valley of Lebanon to Mount Halak. Joshua gave that land to the tribes of Israel as a possession according to their divisions.

l: Sihon, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 12
s: Sihon lived in Heshbon and ruled from Aroer on the edge of the valley of the Arnon, over half of Gilead to the river Jabbok, and the Arabah eastward to the Sea of Chinneroth and the Salt Sea. He was struck by Moses and the children of Israel, and his territory bordered that of Og.

l: Og, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 12
s: Og, of the remnant of the Rephaim, lived at Ashtaroth and Edrei. He ruled in Mount Hermon, Salecah, and all Bashan to the border of the Geshurites and Maacathites, and half Gilead, bordering Sihon. Moses and the children of Israel struck him.

l: kings of the land, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 12
s: The kings west of the Jordan numbered thirty-one in all, each listed as one king of his city, from Jericho and Ai to Tirzah. They ruled the hill country, lowland, Arabah, slopes, wilderness, and South, among the Hittite, Amorite, Canaanite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite, and were struck by Joshua and the children of Israel.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 13
s: Joshua is old, and the LORD tells him that much land remains to be possessed, listing the regions of the Philistines, Geshurites, Canaanites, Sidonians, Gebalites and Lebanon. The LORD promises to drive out the inhabitants and commands Joshua to allocate the land to the nine tribes and the half-tribe of Manasseh. The chapter then recounts the inheritance Moses already gave beyond the Jordan eastward to the Reubenites, the Gadites and the other half-tribe of Manasseh, with detailed border and city lists for each, including the kingdoms of Sihon and Og. It notes that Israel did not drive out the Geshurites and Maacathites, who still live within Israel, and that the tribe of Levi received no land inheritance because the LORD and his offerings are its inheritance.

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 13
s: Joshua is described as old and well advanced in years. The LORD tells him that very much land remains to be possessed and commands him to divide it as an inheritance among the nine tribes and the half-tribe of Manasseh.

l: LORD, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 13
s: The LORD tells Joshua what land remains and promises to drive out its inhabitants from before the children of Israel. He instructs that it be allocated to Israel as an inheritance, and he is himself the inheritance of Levi, with the fire offerings as Levi's portion.

l: Moses, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 13
s: Moses is recalled as having given the Transjordan inheritances to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh in the plains of Moab beyond the Jordan at Jericho. He attacked and drove out Og's remnant of the Rephaim and struck Sihon with the chiefs of Midian, and he gave no inheritance to Levi.

l: Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 13
s: Israel is promised that the LORD will drive out the remaining peoples, and its land is to be allocated by inheritance. The children of Israel killed Balaam son of Beor the soothsayer with the sword, but they did not drive out the Geshurites and Maacathites, who live within Israel to this day.

l: Reubenites, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 13
s: The Reubenites received, with the Gadites, the inheritance Moses gave them east of the Jordan. Their border ran from Aroer by the Arnon valley, including Heshbon, Dibon, Jahaz, Beth Peor and the cities of the plain and Sihon's kingdom, with the Jordan's bank as their boundary.

l: Gadites, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 13
s: The Gadites received land east of the Jordan from Moses according to their families. It included Jazer, the cities of Gilead, half the Ammonite land to Aroer near Rabbah, and places such as Mahanaim, Beth Haram, Beth Nimrah, Succoth and Zaphon, reaching to the sea of Chinnereth.

l: half-tribe of Manasseh, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 13
s: Moses gave one half of Manasseh an inheritance east of the Jordan, while the other half is to receive land west of it under Joshua's division. Its territory ran from Mahanaim through all Bashan and Og's kingdom, including Jair's sixty villages, with half of Gilead, Ashtaroth and Edrei going to the children of Machir.

l: tribe of Levi, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 13
s: The tribe of Levi was given no land inheritance. Instead the offerings of the LORD made by fire, and the LORD, the God of Israel, himself, are its inheritance, as he spoke to them.

l: Canaan land remaining to be possessed, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 13
s: The LORD lists the remaining land as the regions of the Philistines and Geshurites, the land of the Canaanites, the Sidonian Mearah to Aphek, the Gebalites' land and all Lebanon from Baal Gad under Mount Hermon to the entrance of Hamath. Its hill-country inhabitants through the Sidonians will be driven out by the LORD.

l: Transjordan inheritance, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 13
s: The land east of the Jordan was already distributed by Moses to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh, covering the kingdoms of Sihon at Heshbon and Og in Bashan. Geshur and Maacath within it were not driven out, and the distribution took place in the plains of Moab at Jericho.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 14
s: Chapter 14 describes how the children of Israel, through Eleazar the priest, Joshua the son of Nun, and the heads of the fathers' houses, distributed the land of Canaan by lot to nine and a half tribes, as the LORD commanded by Moses. The Levites received no land inheritance, only cities with pasture lands, while Moses had already given the two and a half tribes their inheritance beyond the Jordan. At Gilgal, Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite reminds Joshua of Moses' oath, made after the Kadesh Barnea spying, that the land he walked would be his. Now eighty-five and still strong, Caleb asks for the hill country with its Anakim and fortified cities, and Joshua blesses him and gives him Hebron. Hebron, formerly Kiriath Arba, becomes Caleb's inheritance, and the land has rest from war.

l: Caleb the son of Jephunneh, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 14
s: Caleb came to Joshua at Gilgal with the children of Judah and recalled how he was sent at forty to spy out the land, brought back word as it was in his heart, and wholly followed the LORD while his brothers made the people's hearts melt. Now eighty-five and as strong as before, he asked for the hill country and received Hebron as his inheritance from Joshua, who blessed him.

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 14
s: Joshua, along with Eleazar the priest and the heads of the fathers' houses, distributed the inheritances by lot. At Gilgal he heard Caleb's request, blessed him, and gave him Hebron as an inheritance.

l: Moses, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 14
s: Moses is described as the one through whom the LORD commanded the lot-based division, and as the one who had given the two and a half tribes their inheritance beyond the Jordan. He is called the man of God and the servant of the LORD; he sent Caleb from Kadesh Barnea to spy out the land and swore that the land Caleb walked would be his and his children's forever.

l: LORD, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 14
s: The LORD commanded by Moses that the land be divided by lot, and the children of Israel did as he commanded. He spoke concerning Caleb and Joshua at Kadesh Barnea, kept Caleb alive forty-five years as he had said, and Caleb hopes he will be with him to drive out the Anakim. Caleb is said to have wholly followed him.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 14
s: The children of Israel took their inheritances in the land of Canaan, divided by lot among nine tribes and a half-tribe as the LORD commanded Moses. They gave the Levites no portion except cities to dwell in with pasture lands, and the land then had rest from war.

l: Hebron, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 14
s: Hebron was given by Joshua to Caleb the son of Jephunneh as an inheritance, and it remained his inheritance to this day because he followed the LORD wholeheartedly. Its earlier name was Kiriath Arba, after the greatest man among the Anakim.

l: hill country (Hebron region), The Book of Joshua, Chapter 14
s: Caleb asked Joshua for this hill country, which the LORD had spoken of at Kadesh Barnea. He noted that the Anakim and great fortified cities were there, and hoped to drive them out with the LORD's help.

l: land of Canaan, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 14
s: The land of Canaan is where the children of Israel took their inheritances, distributed by lot by Eleazar, Joshua, and the heads of the fathers' houses. The Levites received only cities in it, and at the chapter's end the land had rest from war.

l: Transjordan inheritance, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 14
s: Inheritances were distributed by lot to nine tribes and a half-tribe in Canaan, while two and a half tribes had theirs beyond the Jordan and the Levites received only cities with pasture lands. Caleb's inheritance was the land he walked, promised by Moses' oath to him and his children forever, and fulfilled in Hebron.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 15
s: Chapter 15 describes the lot given to the tribe of the children of Judah, tracing its south, east, north and west borders from the Salt Sea and the brook of Egypt to the great sea. It then recounts how Caleb the son of Jephunneh received Kiriath Arba (Hebron), drove out the three sons of Anak, and offered his daughter Achsah as wife to whoever took Kiriath Sepher (Debir). Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's brother, took it and married Achsah, who asked her father for springs of water in addition to the southern land and received the upper and lower springs. The chapter lists Judah's cities by region (the South, lowland, hill country and wilderness) with the counts given for each group. It ends by noting that the children of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites of Jerusalem, who still live with them.

l: tribe of Judah, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 15
s: The tribe of the children of Judah receives its lot according to its families, bounded by Edom and the wilderness of Zin in the south and by the great sea in the west. A portion among them is given to Caleb, and a full list of its cities by region is recorded. The tribe could not drive out the Jebusites from Jerusalem, who live with them to this day.

l: Caleb the son of Jephunneh, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 15
s: Caleb is given a portion among the children of Judah, Kiriath Arba (Hebron), according to the LORD's commandment to Joshua. He drove out Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai, the three sons of Anak, and offered his daughter Achsah as wife to whoever took Kiriath Sepher. When Achsah came and asked for a blessing, he gave her the upper and lower springs.

l: Othniel the son of Kenaz, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 15
s: Othniel, identified as the brother of Caleb, took Kiriath Sepher (Debir). In return Caleb gave him his daughter Achsah as wife.

l: Achsah, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 15
s: Achsah is Caleb's daughter, offered as wife to whoever takes Kiriath Sepher, and she is given to Othniel after he takes it. When she came, she had him ask her father for a field, got off her donkey, and asked Caleb for a blessing and springs of water because he had set her in the land of the South. He gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.

l: Jebusites, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 15
s: The Jebusites are the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and Judah's northern border passes by the side of the Jebusite city. The children of Judah could not drive them out, and they live with the children of Judah at Jerusalem to this day.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 15
s: Jerusalem is also called the Jebusite in the boundary description, and the border goes up by the valley of the son of Hinnom to its southern side. The children of Judah could not drive out its Jebusite inhabitants, who still live there with them.

l: Hebron, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 15
s: Hebron, also called Kiriath Arba, is named after the father of Anak and is given to Caleb as his portion among Judah. Caleb drove out the three sons of Anak from it. It is listed again among the hill country cities in the group of nine.

l: Debir, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 15
s: Debir, formerly named Kiriath Sepher, is attacked by Caleb's offer of Achsah to whoever takes it, and Othniel takes it. Its inhabitants are the ones Caleb's challenge targets. Kiriath Sannah is also identified as Debir in the hill country list, and a Debir is also named in the border description near the valley of Achor.

l: Judah's allotment boundaries, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 15
s: The south border runs from the Salt Sea's bay by the ascent of Akrabbim, Zin, Kadesh Barnea, Hezron, Addar, Karka and Azmon to the brook of Egypt and the sea. The east border is the Salt Sea to the end of the Jordan, and the north border runs through Beth Hoglah, Beth Arabah, the stone of Bohan, the valley of Achor, En Shemesh, En Rogel, the valley of Hinnom, Baalah, Mount Seir, Beth Shemesh, Timnah, Ekron and Jabneel to the sea. The west border is the shore of the great sea.

l: city lists of Judah, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 15
s: The chapter lists Judah's cities by region: twenty-nine in the South, fourteen and then sixteen and nine in the lowland groups, plus Ekron, Ashdod and Gaza with their towns and villages. The hill country has eleven, nine, ten, six and two cities in successive groups, and the wilderness has six. Each group is given with its villages.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 16
s: Chapter 16 describes the lot that came out for the children of Joseph, whose territory ran from the Jordan at Jericho up through the hill country to Bethel, then via Luz, the Archites' border at Ataroth, the Japhletites' border, lower Beth Horon and Gezer, ending at the sea. Manasseh and Ephraim, the sons of Joseph, took their inheritance. The chapter then gives the border of the children of Ephraim by families, running from Ataroth Addar to upper Beth Horon, through Michmethath, Taanath Shiloh, Janoah, Ataroth, Naarah and Jericho to the Jordan, and from Tappuah westward along the brook of Kanah to the sea. Ephraim also received cities with their villages set apart within Manasseh's inheritance. The Ephraimites did not drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer, who remained in Ephraim's territory as servants doing forced labor.

l: children of Joseph, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 16
s: The lot came out for the children of Joseph, with a border running from the Jordan at Jericho through the hill country to Bethel, Luz, Ataroth, Beth Horon the lower and Gezer, ending at the sea. Manasseh and Ephraim, the children of Joseph, took their inheritance.

l: children of Ephraim, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 16
s: The children of Ephraim received an inheritance with a defined border according to their families, from Ataroth Addar and upper Beth Horon to the Jordan and the sea. They also received cities with villages set apart within Manasseh's inheritance. They did not drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer.

l: Canaanites, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 16
s: The Canaanites who lived in Gezer were not driven out by the children of Ephraim. They continued to dwell in Ephraim's territory to the time of writing and became servants doing forced labor.

l: Gezer, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 16
s: Gezer is named as a point on the border of the children of Joseph, after lower Beth Horon, before the border ends at the sea. Canaanites lived there and were not driven out by Ephraim, remaining in Ephraim's territory as forced laborers.

l: inheritance of the children of Ephraim, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 16
s: Its eastern border ran from Ataroth Addar to upper Beth Horon, then out westward at Michmethath, around to Taanath Shiloh, past Janoah, to Ataroth, Naarah, Jericho and the Jordan, with another line from Tappuah westward along the brook of Kanah to the sea. It also included cities with their villages set apart within the inheritance of Manasseh's children.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 17
s: Chapter 17 describes the lot of the tribe of Manasseh, Joseph's firstborn. Machir received Gilead and Bashan as a man of war, and the other Manasseh families received their shares. Zelophehad's five daughters, who had no brothers, came to Eleazar, Joshua and the princes and received an inheritance among their father's brothers, as the LORD had commanded Moses. The chapter traces Manasseh's border with Ephraim and lists cities in Issachar and Asher that Manasseh could not drive the Canaanites out of, though Israel later put them to forced labor. The children of Joseph complained to Joshua that they had only one lot, and Joshua told them to clear the forest hill country and drive out the Canaanites despite their iron chariots.

l: Manasseh, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 17
s: Manasseh is identified as Joseph's firstborn, and his son Machir, father of Gilead, received Gilead and Bashan as a man of war. His other families (Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher, Shemida) received lots, and ten parts fell to him besides Gilead and Bashan beyond the Jordan. His children could not drive the Canaanites out of certain cities.

l: children of Joseph, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 17
s: The children of Joseph complained to Joshua that one lot and one part was too little for a numerous people blessed by the LORD. When Joshua told them to clear the forest, they said the hill country was not enough and the valley Canaanites had iron chariots. Joshua, addressing them as the house of Joseph (Ephraim and Manasseh), said they were numerous and powerful and would have the hill country and drive out the Canaanites.

l: Zelophehad, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 17
s: Zelophehad is identified as the son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh. He had no sons, only daughters, who named Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah.

l: daughters of Zelophehad, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 17
s: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah came to Eleazar the priest, Joshua and the princes, citing the LORD's command to Moses that they receive an inheritance among their brothers. According to that command, Joshua gave them an inheritance among their father's brothers.

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 17
s: Joshua gave Zelophehad's daughters an inheritance according to the LORD's commandment. When the children of Joseph complained of having one lot, he told them to clear the forest of the Perizzites and Rephaim, and then assured them the hill country would be theirs if they drove out the strong, iron-chariot Canaanites.

l: Ephraim, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 17
s: Ephraim's territory lay south of Manasseh's along the brook of Kanah, and Ephraim held Tappuah on Manasseh's border and some cities among Manasseh's cities. Ephraim is named with Manasseh as the house of Joseph, whose hill country was said to be too narrow for them.

l: Canaanites, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 17
s: The Canaanites remained in the cities Manasseh could not take, including Beth Shean, Ibleam, Dor, Endor, Taanach and Megiddo. When Israel grew strong they were put to forced labor rather than utterly driven out. The children of Joseph noted the valley Canaanites had iron chariots, and Joshua said they would be driven out regardless.

l: inheritance allotment of Manasseh, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 17
s: Manasseh's allotment included Gilead and Bashan beyond the Jordan plus ten parts west of it, with the daughters of Zelophehad receiving shares among their father's brothers. Its border ran from Asher to Michmethath near Shechem, down to the brook of Kanah, with Ephraim to the south, Asher to the north, Issachar to the east, and the sea as boundary. It also included towns in Issachar and Asher such as Beth Shean, Ibleam, Dor, Endor, Taanach and Megiddo.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 18
s: The whole congregation of Israel assembled at Shiloh and set up the Tent of Meeting, as the land lay subdued before them. Joshua rebuked the seven tribes that had not yet received inheritances and directed them to appoint three men from each tribe to survey the land in seven portions and bring a written description back to him. The surveyors recorded the land by cities in a book, and Joshua cast lots for the tribes before the LORD at Shiloh. The first lot to come up was for the tribe of Benjamin, whose borders on the north, west, south, and east are described in detail, lying between Judah and the children of Joseph. The chapter closes by listing Benjamin's twenty-six cities in two groups, twelve and fourteen, with their villages.

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 18
s: Joshua rebuked the children of Israel for neglecting to possess the land and instructed them to appoint three men per tribe to survey it in seven portions. He sent the surveyors out, received their written description at Shiloh, and cast lots for the tribes before the LORD, dividing the land according to their divisions.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 18
s: The whole congregation of the children of Israel assembled at Shiloh and set up the Tent of Meeting there. They were told by Joshua to appoint three men from each tribe for surveying the land, and the land was then divided among them by lot.

l: Shiloh, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 18
s: Shiloh was where the congregation assembled and set up the Tent of Meeting. It was the place where the surveyors reported to Joshua at the camp and where Joshua cast lots before the LORD to divide the remaining land.

l: tribe of Benjamin, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 18
s: The tribe of Benjamin received the first lot cast at Shiloh, according to its families. Its territory lay between the children of Judah and the children of Joseph, and it was given twenty-six cities with their villages.

l: seven tribes, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 18
s: Seven tribes had not yet divided their inheritance, and Joshua urged them to stop delaying in taking possession of the land. Their portions were to be surveyed in seven parts and assigned by lot at Shiloh, with Judah staying in the south and the house of Joseph in the north.

l: surveyors (men appointed from each tribe), The Book of Joshua, Chapter 18
s: Three men from each tribe were appointed to walk through the land and describe it according to their inheritance. They went out, surveyed it by cities into seven portions in a book, and returned to Joshua at the camp at Shiloh.

l: land of Canaan, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 18
s: The land is described as subdued before Israel and as given by the LORD, the God of their fathers. It was surveyed into seven portions for the remaining tribes, while the Levites received no portion and Gad, Reuben, and the half-tribe of Manasseh already held land east of the Jordan.

l: casting of lots, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 18
s: Joshua cast lots for the seven portions in Shiloh before the LORD to divide the land among the tribes. The first lot to come up was that of the tribe of Benjamin.

l: Benjamin's borders and territory, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 18
s: Benjamin's north border ran from the Jordan by Jericho through the hill country to the wilderness of Beth Aven, Luz (Bethel), and Ataroth Addar near lower Beth Horon. The west ended at Kiriath Jearim, the south ran by the spring of Nephtoah, the valley of Hinnom, En Rogel, and the stone of Bohan to the north bay of the Salt Sea, and the Jordan formed the east border. Its cities included Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon, Ramah, and the Jebusite city (Jerusalem), in groups of twelve and fourteen.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 19
s: Chapter 19 records the last allotments of land by lot among the remaining tribes. Simeon receives the second lot, taking cities within Judah's territory because Judah's portion was too large. Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan receive the third through seventh lots, each with borders and cities listed. The Danites expand by capturing Leshem and renaming it Dan. The children of Israel then give Joshua the city Timnathserah in Ephraim's hill country, and Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the heads of the fathers' houses finish dividing the land by lot at Shiloh before the LORD.

l: tribe of Simeon, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 19
s: The second lot came out for the tribe of Simeon, whose inheritance lay in the middle of Judah's. It received thirteen cities with villages (Beersheba, Moladah, Ziklag, Sharuhen and others) plus four more (Ain, Rimmon, Ether, Ashan), and the villages around them as far as Baalath Beer, Ramah of the South.

l: tribe of Judah, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 19
s: Judah's portion proved too large for the tribe, so part of it was given to Simeon, who received an inheritance in the middle of Judah's land. Judah's border at the Jordan toward the sunrise also marks the edge of Naphtali's territory.

l: tribe of Zebulun, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 19
s: The third lot came up for Zebulun, with a border running from Sarid west to Maralah and Dabbesheth, then east to Chisloth Tabor, Daberath, Japhia, Gath Hepher, Rimmon and Hannathon, ending at the valley of Iphtah El. Its inheritance was twelve cities with their villages, including Kattath, Nahalal, Shimron, Idalah and Bethlehem.

l: tribe of Issachar, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 19
s: The fourth lot came out for Issachar, whose border included Jezreel, Chesulloth, Shunem and other towns, reaching Tabor, Shahazumah and Beth Shemesh and ending at the Jordan. Its inheritance was sixteen cities with their villages.

l: tribe of Asher, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 19
s: The fifth lot came out for Asher, whose border included Helkath, Hali, Beten and Achshaph, reaching Carmel on the west, touching Zebulun and the valley of Iphtah El, and extending to great Sidon, Tyre and the sea by Achzib. Its inheritance was twenty-two cities with their villages.

l: Naphtali, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 19
s: The sixth lot came out for Naphtali, whose border ran from Heleph and the oak in Zaanannim to Lakkum and the Jordan, then west to Aznoth Tabor and Hukkok. It touched Zebulun on the south, Asher on the west and Judah at the Jordan, and had nineteen cities with villages, including the fortified cities Ziddim, Hammath, Chinnereth and Hazor.

l: tribe of Dan, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 19
s: The seventh lot came out for Dan, with cities such as Zorah, Eshtaol, Aijalon, Timnah and Ekron, and a border opposite Joppa. The Danites went beyond their border, fought Leshem, took it and lived there, naming it Dan after their forefather.

l: Leshem, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 19
s: Leshem was attacked by the children of Dan, who struck it with the edge of the sword, took it, possessed it and lived in it. They renamed it Dan after their forefather.

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 19
s: After the land was distributed, the children of Israel gave Joshua the son of Nun an inheritance among them. According to the LORD's commandment he received the city he asked for, Timnathserah in Ephraim's hill country, where he built the city and lived. He is also named among those who distributed the inheritances by lot at Shiloh.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 19
s: The children of Israel finished distributing the land by its borders and gave Joshua the city he asked for, Timnathserah. Their leaders completed the division by lot at Shiloh before the LORD, at the door of the Tent of Meeting.

l: lot distribution of the land, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 19
s: The lots for the remaining tribes were cast in order: second Simeon, third Zebulun, fourth Issachar, fifth Asher, sixth Naphtali and seventh Dan. Eleazar the priest, Joshua and the heads of the fathers' houses distributed the inheritances by lot at Shiloh before the LORD, at the door of the Tent of Meeting, and so finished dividing the land.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 20
s: The LORD tells Joshua to instruct the children of Israel to assign the cities of refuge, as previously spoken of through Moses, so that someone who kills a person accidentally can flee from the avenger of blood. The text sets out the procedure: the man slayer declares his case to the elders at the city gate, is given a place to live, and is not handed over to the avenger of blood. He stays there until he stands before the congregation for judgment and until the death of the high priest, after which he may return to his own city and house. Three cities west of the Jordan (Kedesh, Shechem, Kiriath Arba/Hebron) and three beyond the Jordan (Bezer, Ramoth, Golan) are set apart. These cities serve all the children of Israel and the alien living among them.

l: LORD, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 20
s: The LORD spoke to Joshua and commanded that the cities of refuge be assigned, referring to what he had earlier spoken through Moses. He specified the rules by which an unintentional killer is protected from the avenger of blood.

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 20
s: Joshua receives the LORD's word and is told to speak to the children of Israel about assigning the cities of refuge. He acts as the intermediary of this command.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 20
s: The children of Israel are commanded to assign the cities of refuge and set apart Kedesh, Shechem, Kiriath Arba, Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan. The cities are appointed for all of them and for the alien living among them.

l: cities of refuge (for the man slayer), The Book of Joshua, Chapter 20
s: The cities of refuge are assigned as places where an unintentional killer may flee from the avenger of blood. Six are named: Kedesh in Naphtali, Shechem in Ephraim, Kiriath Arba (Hebron) in Judah, Bezer from Reuben, Ramoth in Gilead from Gad, and Golan in Bashan from Manasseh. Their elders hear the fugitive's case, take him in, and give him a place to live.

l: man slayer (unintentional killer), The Book of Joshua, Chapter 20
s: The man slayer who killed someone accidentally or unintentionally may flee to a city of refuge, declare his case to the elders at the gate, and be given a place to live. He dwells there until he stands before the congregation for judgment and until the high priest dies, then may return to his own city and house.

l: avenger of blood, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 20
s: The avenger of blood is the one from whom the cities of refuge give protection. If he pursues the man slayer, the city's people must not hand the man over to him, because the man struck his neighbor unintentionally and did not hate him before.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 21
s: The heads of the Levite families approach Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the tribal heads at Shiloh, reminding them that the LORD commanded through Moses that cities with pasture lands be given to the Levites. The Israelites give cities by lot out of their inheritance: thirteen to the priestly children of Aaron among the Kohathites, ten to the rest of the Kohathites, thirteen to the Gershonites, and twelve to the Merarites. The chapter lists each city by name and tribe, marking the cities of refuge (Hebron, Shechem, Golan, Kedesh, Ramoth in Gilead), and notes that Caleb son of Jephunneh keeps the fields and villages of Hebron. The total comes to forty-eight cities with their pasture lands. The chapter closes by declaring that the LORD gave Israel all the land he swore to their fathers, granted rest on every side, and that nothing he promised failed.

l: Levites, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 21
s: The heads of the Levite families come to Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal heads at Shiloh to request the cities the LORD commanded through Moses. They receive forty-eight cities with pasture lands from the other tribes' inheritance, divided among the Kohathites, Gershonites, and Merarites.

l: Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 21
s: The children of Israel give the Levites cities with pasture lands out of their own inheritance, according to the LORD's commandment. They then possess and live in all the land, enjoy rest on every side, and see no enemy stand against them.

l: LORD, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 21
s: The LORD is the one who commanded through Moses that the Levites receive cities, and he gives Israel all the land he swore to their fathers. He gives them rest all around and delivers all their enemies into their hand, so that nothing he spoke fails.

l: Kohathites, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 21
s: The Kohathites receive the first lot, and their share totals twenty-three cities. The children of Aaron among them receive thirteen cities, and the rest of the Kohathites receive ten out of Ephraim, Dan, and the half-tribe of Manasseh.

l: children of Aaron the priest, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 21
s: The children of Aaron, of the Kohathite families, receive thirteen cities out of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin by the first lot. These include Hebron, a city of refuge, though the fields and villages of Hebron go to Caleb.

l: Gershonites, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 21
s: The Gershonites receive thirteen cities by lot out of Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and the half-tribe of Manasseh in Bashan. Golan in Bashan and Kedesh in Galilee are among them as cities of refuge.

l: Merarites, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 21
s: The Merarites, described as the rest of the Levites, receive twelve cities out of Zebulun, Reuben, and Gad. Ramoth in Gilead, a city of refuge, is among them.

l: cities of the Levites, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 21
s: The Levites hold forty-eight cities in all, each with its surrounding pasture lands. Five of them, Hebron, Shechem, Golan, Kedesh in Galilee, and Ramoth in Gilead, are named as cities of refuge for the man slayer.

l: Allotment of cities by lot, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 21
s: The cities are distributed to the Levite families by lot, as the LORD commanded by Moses. The first lot falls to the Kohathite children of Aaron, followed by the rest of the Kohathites, the Gershonites, and the Merarites.

l: land of Canaan, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 21
s: The chapter states that the LORD gave Israel all the land he swore to give to their fathers, and that they possessed it and lived in it. It is presented as the fulfillment of the LORD's promise, with all of it coming to pass.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 22
s: Joshua commends the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh for keeping all that Moses and he commanded, blesses them, and sends them home to their land beyond the Jordan. After they build a great altar by the Jordan, the children of Israel gather at Shiloh to go to war against them, but first send Phinehas son of Eleazar with ten princes to accuse them of rebellion. The eastern tribes answer that the altar is not for sacrifice but a witness, so that future generations will not say they have no portion in the LORD. Phinehas and the princes are pleased, the war is called off, and the altar is named "A Witness Between Us that the LORD is God."

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 22
s: Joshua calls the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh, praises them for keeping all that Moses and he commanded, and charges them to love the LORD and keep his law. He blesses them, tells them to return with great wealth and share the plunder with their brothers, and sends them to their tents. He is also noted as having given the other half of Manasseh an inheritance west of the Jordan.

l: Reubenites, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 22
s: The Reubenites are released by Joshua and return to Gilead, where together with Gad and Manasseh they build a great altar by the Jordan. Accused of rebellion by Israel's delegation, they explain it is a witness and not for sacrifice, and they name it "A Witness Between Us that the LORD is God."

l: Gadites, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 22
s: The Gadites are sent home by Joshua and return to Gilead, where with Reuben and Manasseh they build a great altar by the Jordan. They defend it as a witness rather than a place of sacrifice, and are vindicated by Phinehas; with Reuben they name the altar "A Witness Between Us that the LORD is God."

l: half-tribe of Manasseh, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 22
s: The half-tribe of Manasseh is sent away by Joshua with a blessing; its other half already held land in Bashan from Moses, while this half was given land west of the Jordan. They return with Reuben and Gad, help build the great altar, and are cleared of the charge of trespass after explaining its purpose.

l: LORD, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 22
s: The LORD is the God whom Joshua exhorts the eastern tribes to love, serve, and hold fast to, and who has given rest to Israel's brothers as he promised. Israel fears his anger over the altar, recalling Peor and Achan. Phinehas concludes that he is among them because the trespass was not committed.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 22
s: The children of Israel hear that an altar has been built and gather at Shiloh to go to war against the eastern tribes. They first send Phinehas and ten princes to confront them, citing the iniquity of Peor and Achan's trespass. Satisfied by the explanation, they bless God and abandon the plan for war.

l: Phinehas, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 22
s: Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest leads the delegation of ten princes to Gilead to charge the eastern tribes with rebellion. After hearing their explanation he is pleased and declares that the LORD is among them and that they have delivered Israel from the LORD's hand. He returns to Canaan and reports to the children of Israel.

l: altar (built by Reuben, Gad and Manasseh), The Book of Joshua, Chapter 22
s: The altar is a great one built beside the Jordan in the region of Canaan, which provokes Israel to prepare for war. Its builders say it is a copy of the LORD's altar, meant as a witness and not for burnt offering or sacrifice. It is named "A Witness Between Us that the LORD is God."

l: Jordan, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 22
s: The Jordan is the boundary between the eastern tribes' land and the rest of Israel's land. The altar is built in the region by the Jordan, and the eastern tribes fear later generations will say the river leaves them no portion in the LORD.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 23
s: After the LORD gave Israel rest from their enemies, the aged Joshua gathered Israel's elders, heads, judges, and officers to give a farewell charge. He reminded them that the LORD fought for them and that the remaining nations were allotted to them as an inheritance, to be driven out by the LORD. He urged them to keep all that is written in the book of the law of Moses, to hold fast to the LORD, to avoid the gods of the remaining nations, and to love the LORD. He warned that intermarriage with these nations would make them a snare and a trap and cause the LORD to stop driving them out. Noting that he was going the way of all the earth, he said that every good promise had been fulfilled and that disobeying the covenant and serving other gods would bring destruction from the good land.

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 23
s: Joshua, old and well advanced in years, called together all Israel's elders, heads, judges, and officers to address them. He urged courage, faithfulness to the law, and love for the LORD, and warned of the consequences of turning away. He stated that he was going the way of all the earth.

l: LORD, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 23
s: The LORD gave Israel rest from their enemies, fought for them, and drove great and strong nations out before them. Joshua says not one of his good promises has failed, and that he will drive out the remaining nations. If Israel disobeys the covenant, his anger will be kindled and he will bring evil things on them until they are destroyed from the land.

l: Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 23
s: Israel received rest from their enemies and had seen the LORD fight for them, so that no man had stood before them. They are charged to be courageous, keep the law, hold fast to the LORD, and not mingle with the remaining nations. They are warned that disobedience would lead them to perish quickly from the good land.

l: nations (remaining among Israel), The Book of Joshua, Chapter 23
s: The remaining nations were allotted to Israel as an inheritance, and the LORD would thrust them out and drive them from Israel's sight. Israel was told not to come among them, mention their gods, swear by them, serve them, or bow down to them. If Israel held fast to them, they would become a snare, a trap, a scourge in the sides, and thorns in the eyes.

l: book of the law of Moses, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 23
s: Joshua tells Israel to be very courageous to keep and do all that is written in the book of the law of Moses. They are not to turn from it to the right hand or to the left.

l: good land (Israel's land), The Book of Joshua, Chapter 23
s: The land is described as good and as given by the LORD to Israel. Joshua warns that if Israel disobeys, they will perish quickly from off this good land. The land is thus the stake in Israel's obedience.

l: covenant of the LORD, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 23
s: The covenant is something the LORD commanded Israel. Joshua says that disobeying it by going to serve and bow down to other gods will kindle the LORD's anger and cause Israel to perish from the land.

l: intermarriage with the nations, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 23
s: Joshua warns that going back and holding fast to the remnant of the nations by making marriages with them would bring severe consequences. The LORD would no longer drive those nations out, and they would become a snare, a trap, a scourge, and thorns until Israel perishes from the good land.

l: warning of destruction for disobedience, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 23
s: Joshua states that just as all the good things the LORD spoke have come, so he will bring all the evil things if Israel disobeys. If they break the covenant and serve other gods, they will be destroyed from the good land. He says the LORD's anger will be kindled and they will perish quickly.

l: The Book of Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 24
s: Joshua gathers all the tribes of Israel, with their elders, heads, judges, and officers, at Shechem, where they present themselves before God. Speaking for the LORD, he recounts the history from Terah and Abraham through the Exodus, the wilderness, the conquest of the Amorites, and the gift of the land. He calls the people to put away foreign gods and serve the LORD, declaring that he and his house will do so. The people pledge to serve the LORD, Joshua warns that the LORD is holy and jealous, and he makes a covenant, writes the words in the book of the law, and sets up a great stone as witness. The chapter closes with the deaths and burials of Joshua at Timnathserah and Eleazar, and the burial of Joseph's bones at Shechem.

l: Joshua, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 24
s: Joshua assembles Israel at Shechem, delivers the LORD's recital of his acts, and challenges the people to choose whom to serve, declaring that he and his house will serve the LORD. He warns the people, makes a covenant, writes the words in the book of the law, and sets up a stone as witness before sending them to their inheritances. He then dies at 110 years old and is buried in Timnathserah in the hill country of Ephraim.

l: LORD, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 24
s: The LORD, through Joshua, recounts how he took Abraham from beyond the River, brought Israel out of Egypt, defeated the Amorites and other peoples with the hornet, and gave a land they had not labored for. Joshua describes him as a holy and jealous God who will not forgive disobedience and will turn and do evil to those who forsake him. Israel serves him throughout the days of Joshua and the elders who outlived him.

l: Israel, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 24
s: Israel's tribes, elders, heads, judges, and officers gather at Shechem and hear the history of the LORD's deliverance. The people repeatedly vow to serve the LORD, declare themselves witnesses against themselves, and agree to put away foreign gods. They serve the LORD all the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him, and they bury Joseph's bones at Shechem.

l: Shechem, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 24
s: Shechem is the place where Joshua gathers all the tribes and where the covenant, statute, and ordinance are made. The great stone is set up there under the oak by the LORD's sanctuary. Joseph's bones, brought up out of Egypt, are buried there in the parcel Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor for a hundred pieces of silver, and it becomes the inheritance of Joseph's children.

l: gods (of the nations), The Book of Joshua, Chapter 24
s: The gods served by the fathers beyond the River and in Egypt, and the gods of the Amorites, are named as the alternatives to the LORD. Joshua tells the people to put them away and warns that serving foreign gods will bring the LORD's judgment. The people reject them, saying far be it from them to forsake the LORD to serve other gods.

l: covenant at Shechem, The Book of Joshua, Chapter 24
s: Joshua makes a covenant with the people at Shechem after they promise to serve the LORD and listen to his voice, and he sets for them a statute and an ordinance. He records the words in the book of the law of God and sets up a great stone under the oak by the LORD's sanctuary as a witness against them, lest they deny their God.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 1
s: King David is old and cannot keep warm, so his servants bring Abishag the Shunammite to attend him. His son Adonijah declares himself king and holds a feast with Joab and Abiathar the priest, omitting Nathan, Benaiah, the mighty men, and Solomon. Nathan and Bathsheba each go to David, reminding him of his oath that Solomon would reign, and David orders Solomon anointed at Gihon by Zadok and Nathan. The people celebrate Solomon's kingship, Adonijah's guests scatter on hearing the news, and Adonijah clings to the altar's horns in fear. Solomon promises Adonijah safety if he proves worthy, then sends him home.

l: David, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 1
s: David is old and cannot keep warm, and he does not know that Adonijah has made himself king. After hearing Bathsheba and Nathan, he vows to fulfill his oath that Solomon will reign and commands that Solomon be anointed king at Gihon. He blesses the LORD for letting him see a successor seated on his throne.

l: Adonijah, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 1
s: Adonijah, son of Haggith, exalts himself, saying "I will be king," and gathers chariots, horsemen, and support from Joab and Abiathar. He holds a feast for his brothers and the men of Judah, but when Solomon is anointed his guests flee, and he grabs the altar's horns in fear. Solomon spares him conditionally, saying he will be safe if he shows himself worthy, and sends him home.

l: Nathan, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 1
s: Nathan the prophet was not with Adonijah and was not invited to his feast. He advises Bathsheba to remind David of his oath about Solomon, then comes in to confirm her words. He then helps anoint Solomon king at Gihon.

l: Solomon, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 1
s: Solomon is not invited to Adonijah's feast, but David, recalling his oath, orders him to ride the king's mule to Gihon. There Zadok anoints him, the people proclaim "Long live King Solomon!", and he sits on the throne. He then promises Adonijah safety if he proves worthy and tells him to go to his house.

l: Bathsheba, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 1
s: Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, is warned by Nathan that Adonijah reigns and that her life and Solomon's are at risk. She goes to David and reminds him of his oath that Solomon would reign, saying she and Solomon will otherwise be considered criminals. David affirms the oath to her, and she bows and wishes him to live forever.

l: succession to David's throne, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 1
s: The succession is contested: Adonijah claims the throne with the backing of Joab and Abiathar, while David had sworn that Solomon would reign after him. David settles it by having Solomon anointed at Gihon and seated on the throne. Adonijah's supporters disperse, and Adonijah submits to Solomon.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 2
