s: As David nears death he charges his son Solomon to keep the LORD's law and to deal with Joab and Shimei while rewarding the sons of Barzillai. David dies after reigning forty years, and Solomon's kingdom is established. Adonijah asks Bathsheba to request Abishag as his wife, and Solomon takes this as a threat and has Benaiah kill him. Solomon banishes Abiathar from the priesthood, has Benaiah kill Joab at the altar, and installs Benaiah over the army and Zadok as priest. Shimei is confined to Jerusalem, leaves for Gath to retrieve runaway slaves, and is put to death by Benaiah on Solomon's order.

l: David, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: Near death, David charges Solomon to keep the LORD's law and to deal with Joab and Shimei, and to show kindness to the sons of Barzillai. He dies, is buried in David's city, and is said to have reigned forty years: seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem.

l: Solomon, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: Solomon takes David's throne and his kingdom is firmly established. He has Adonijah and Joab killed, removes Abiathar from the priesthood, appoints Benaiah over the army and Zadok as priest, and has Shimei killed for breaking his confinement. He honors his mother Bathsheba by seating her at his right hand.

l: Joab, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: David names Joab's killing of Abner and Amasa as a reason he should not die in peace. Having followed Adonijah, Joab flees to the LORD's Tent and holds the altar's horns, refuses to come out, and is killed there by Benaiah on Solomon's order. He is buried in his own house in the wilderness.

l: Shimei, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: David recalls that Shimei cursed him but was sworn not to be killed by the sword, and tells Solomon to bring his gray head down to Sheol with blood. Solomon confines him to Jerusalem on pain of death; after three years he crosses to Gath to retrieve two runaway slaves, and Benaiah kills him on Solomon's command.

l: Adonijah, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: Adonijah, who says the kingdom had been his, asks Bathsheba to request Abishag the Shunammite as his wife. Solomon treats the request as speaking against his own life and has Benaiah kill him.

l: Bathsheba, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: Bathsheba agrees to carry Adonijah's request for Abishag to King Solomon. Solomon bows to her and seats her at his right hand, but he refuses the request and condemns Adonijah.

l: Benaiah, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, carries out Solomon's orders to kill Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei. He is rewarded by being put in Joab's place over the army.

l: Abiathar, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: Solomon says Abiathar deserves death but spares him because he bore the ark before David and shared his afflictions. He is sent to his fields at Anathoth and removed as priest, fulfilling the LORD's word about the house of Eli, and Zadok replaces him.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: The LORD is invoked in David's charge, in the promise of a man on Israel's throne for careful descendants, and in Solomon's oaths. The text says his word about the house of Eli is fulfilled by Abiathar's removal, and that he will return blood on the heads of Joab and Shimei and bring peace to David's house forever.

l: Jerusalem, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: David reigns thirty-three years in Jerusalem, and Shimei is ordered to build a house and live there without leaving. Shimei lives there many days until his trip to Gath.

l: Gath, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: Two of Shimei's slaves run away to Achish, son of Maacah, king of Gath. Shimei goes there and brings them back, and this trip breaks Solomon's restriction and leads to his death.

l: David’s charge to Solomon, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 2
s: David urges Solomon to be strong, keep the LORD's law, and act wisely so that the promise of a man on the throne holds. He directs Solomon not to let Joab die in peace, to show kindness to Barzillai's sons, and to bring Shimei down to Sheol with blood. Solomon goes on to act on the instructions concerning Joab and Shimei.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: Solomon allies with Pharaoh of Egypt by marrying his daughter, and the people still sacrifice at high places while Solomon, who loves the LORD, does the same at Gibeon. There the LORD appears to him in a dream and invites him to ask for something; Solomon requests an understanding heart to judge God's people. The LORD is pleased, grants wisdom plus riches and honor, and promises long life if Solomon obeys. Back in Jerusalem, Solomon offers sacrifices and holds a feast, then judges between two prostitutes who both claim a living child, ordering it divided by sword and discerning the true mother by her compassion. All Israel hears of the judgment and fears the king, seeing God's wisdom in him.

l: Solomon, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: Solomon allies with Pharaoh by marrying his daughter, sacrifices at the Gibeon high place, and in a dream asks the LORD for an understanding heart. After waking he offers sacrifices in Jerusalem and holds a feast. He then settles the dispute between two women by ordering the living child divided, identifying the true mother, and thereby earns the awe of all Israel.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: The LORD appears to Solomon in a dream at Gibeon and invites him to ask for what he wishes. Pleased by the request, he grants a wise and understanding heart unmatched before or after, adds riches and honor, and promises to lengthen Solomon's days if he walks in his ways as David did.

l: Solomon's dream at Gibeon, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: After Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings at Gibeon, the LORD appears to him by night in a dream and tells him to ask for what he should be given. The dream contains Solomon's request, God's gift of wisdom, riches and honor, and a conditional promise of long life. Solomon awakes and recognizes it was a dream.

l: Solomon's request for an understanding heart, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: Solomon, calling himself a little child who does not know how to go out or come in, asks for an understanding heart to judge God's great people and discern good from evil. He passes over long life, riches, and the death of enemies. The request pleases the LORD.

l: first woman (the living child's mother), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: She tells the king that she and the other woman lived in one house and gave birth three days apart, and that the other woman took her living son at midnight and put her dead child in her bosom. When the king orders the child divided, her heart yearns over her son and she begs that he be given to the other woman rather than killed. The king declares her the mother.

l: other woman (mother of the dead child), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: Her child died in the night because she lay on it. She is accused of switching the babies, and she insists the living child is hers. When the king orders the living child divided, she says he should be neither's and demands the division, so the child is given to the first woman.

l: living child, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: The living child is claimed by both women and is ordered by the king to be divided in two with a sword. He is spared when the first woman pleads for his life, and the king gives him to her as his mother.

l: dead child, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: The dead child died in the night when his mother lay on him. According to the first woman, he was placed in her bosom in place of her living son, and she recognized in the morning that he was not hers.

l: Solomon's judgment, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: Solomon has a sword brought and commands that the living child be divided between the two women. Their opposite reactions reveal the true mother, and he orders the child given to the one who pleaded to spare him. All Israel hears of it and fears the king.

l: wisdom of God, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 3
s: The wisdom of God is what the people of Israel see in Solomon after his judgment, and it is understood as enabling him to do justice. It reflects the wise and understanding heart the LORD gave him in answer to his request.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: Chapter 4 lists King Solomon's princes and officials, including Azariah, Zadok, Abiathar, Benaiah, Ahishar, and Adoniram, who held posts over priests, scribes, the army, the household, and forced labor. It names the twelve officers who each provisioned the king and his household for one month a year across Israel, including Ben Hur, Baana, Ahimaaz, and Geber. The chapter describes Solomon's wide dominion from the River to the border of Egypt, the peace and prosperity of Judah and Israel, his large daily provision, and his forty thousand stalls of horses and twelve thousand horsemen. It closes by praising the wisdom God gave Solomon, which surpassed that of the east and Egypt, including his three thousand proverbs and one thousand five songs, and says people of all nations came to hear him.

l: Solomon, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: King Solomon is king over all Israel, with a list of princes and officials serving him. He rules over all the kingdoms from the River to the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt, receives tribute, and has peace on all sides. He keeps forty thousand stalls of horses and twelve thousand horsemen, and is renowned for his wisdom, proverbs, and songs.

l: Israel, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: Israel, together with Judah, is described as numerous as the sand by the sea, eating, drinking, and making merry. The people live safely, each man under his vine and fig tree, from Dan to Beersheba all the days of Solomon. The land is divided among twelve officers who provision the king.

l: twelve officers (Solomon's officers), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: Solomon has twelve officers over all Israel, each responsible for providing food for the king and his household for one month of the year. They are named with their districts, such as Ben Hur in the hill country of Ephraim, Ahimaaz in Naphtali, and Geber in Gilead, and two of them, Ben Abinadab and Ahimaaz, are married to daughters of Solomon. They also supply food for all who come to Solomon's table, letting nothing be lacking, and bring barley and straw for the horses.

l: Solomon's daily provision, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: Solomon's provision for one day is thirty cors of fine flour, sixty measures of meal, ten fat cattle, twenty pasture-fed cattle, and one hundred sheep. It also includes deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened fowl. The twelve officers supply it month by month.

l: Solomon's wisdom, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 4
s: God gives Solomon abundant wisdom, understanding, and breadth of mind like the sand on the seashore. It excels that of all the children of the east and of Egypt, and he is wiser than Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Darda. He speaks three thousand proverbs, composes one thousand five songs, and speaks of trees, animals, birds, creeping things, and fish, so that people sent by kings of all nations come to hear him.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: Hiram, king of Tyre, sends servants to Solomon after hearing he has been anointed king in place of David, whom Hiram had always loved. Solomon tells Hiram that David could not build a house for the LORD's name because of surrounding wars, but that the LORD has now given him rest, so he intends to build it and asks for cedar cut in Lebanon. Hiram rejoices, blesses the LORD for giving David a wise son, and agrees to supply cedar and cypress timber, floating it by sea in rafts, while Solomon provides yearly wheat and oil for Hiram's household. The two make a treaty, and Solomon raises a levy of thirty thousand men, working in monthly shifts in Lebanon under Adoniram, along with seventy thousand burden bearers, eighty thousand stone cutters, and three thousand three hundred chief officers. Solomon's builders, Hiram's builders, and the Gebalites cut the large, costly stones and prepare timber and stones for the house's foundation.

l: Hiram, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: Hiram, king of Tyre, sent servants to Solomon on hearing of his anointing, having always loved David. He rejoiced at Solomon's message, blessed the LORD for giving David a wise son, and agreed to supply cedar and cypress timber, bringing it down from Lebanon to the sea and floating it in rafts to the place Solomon specified. In return he received yearly wheat and oil for his household, and he made a treaty with Solomon; his builders also helped cut stones and prepare timber.

l: Solomon, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: Solomon, anointed king in place of his father David, wrote to Hiram explaining his intention to build a house for the LORD's name and requesting cedar from Lebanon, offering wages and his servants' help. He paid Hiram twenty thousand cors of wheat and twenty cors of pure oil year by year, and the LORD gave him wisdom as promised. He raised a levy of thirty thousand men, kept seventy thousand burden bearers and eighty thousand stone cutters, and commanded that large costly stones be cut for the foundation.

l: David, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: David is described as Solomon's father, whom Hiram had always loved. Solomon explains that David could not build a house for the LORD's name because of the wars on every side until the LORD put his enemies under his feet. The LORD had promised David that his son, set on his throne, would build the house.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: The LORD is said to have given Solomon rest on every side, with no enemy and no evil occurrence. He had spoken to David that his son would build a house for his name, and he gave Solomon wisdom as he promised. Hiram blessed him for giving David a wise son to rule the great people.

l: Lebanon, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: Lebanon is the place where cedar trees are to be cut for Solomon's building project, with Solomon's servants working alongside Hiram's. Hiram's servants bring the timber down from Lebanon to the sea. Solomon sent his levy there in shifts of ten thousand men per month, one month in Lebanon and two at home.

l: house of the LORD (the temple Solomon built), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: Solomon announces his intention to build this house for the name of the LORD, fulfilling the LORD's word to David that his son would build it. Preparations begin with timber from Hiram and large, costly worked stones cut for its foundation. Solomon's builders, Hiram's builders, and the Gebalites prepare the timber and stones.

l: cedar and cypress timber, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: Solomon requests cedar from Lebanon, and Hiram agrees to provide cedar and cypress timber according to all Solomon's desire. It is to be brought down to the sea, made into rafts, floated to the place Solomon specifies, and broken up there for him to receive. Hiram gave the timber, and in exchange Solomon supplied wheat and oil for Hiram's household.

l: levy of forced laborers (Solomon's levy), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 5
s: Solomon raised a levy of thirty thousand men out of all Israel and sent them to Lebanon in courses of ten thousand a month, one month there and two at home. Adoniram was over the men subject to forced labor. Alongside them Solomon had seventy thousand burden bearers, eighty thousand stone cutters in the mountains, and three thousand three hundred chief officers ruling the laborers.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: Chapter 6 describes King Solomon building the LORD's house in the fourth year of his reign, 480 years after Israel left Egypt. The text gives the dimensions of the house, porch, and side rooms, and notes that the stone was prepared at the quarry so no iron tool was heard on site. The LORD speaks to Solomon, promising to establish his word and dwell among Israel if Solomon keeps his statutes and commandments. The interior is lined with carved cedar and overlaid with gold, and an inner sanctuary is prepared for the ark of the LORD's covenant, containing two ten-cubit olive-wood cherubim overlaid with gold. The foundation was laid in the month Ziv of the fourth year and the house was finished in the month Bul of the eleventh year, a span of seven years.

l: Solomon, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: Solomon, in the fourth year of his reign over Israel, began to build the LORD's house and finished it after seven years. He received the LORD's word promising to establish his word if he walked in the LORD's statutes, ordinances, and commandments. He lined the interior with cedar, overlaid it with gold, made the cherubim and the olive-wood doors, and built the inner court.

l: the LORD, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: The LORD spoke to Solomon, saying that if Solomon walks in his statutes, executes his ordinances, and keeps his commandments, he will establish his word, which he spoke to David, Solomon's father. He also promised to dwell among the children of Israel and not forsake his people Israel.

l: house of the LORD (the temple Solomon built), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: The house was sixty cubits long, twenty wide, and thirty high, with a porch twenty cubits long and ten wide in front, lattice windows, and side rooms on three floors around its walls. It was built of stone prepared at the quarry, covered with cedar beams and planks, lined inside with cedar, and overlaid with gold. Its foundation was laid in Ziv of the fourth year and it was finished in Bul of the eleventh year.

l: inner sanctuary (the LORD's house), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: The inner sanctuary was prepared at the back of the house, twenty cubits in length, width, and height, to hold the ark of the LORD's covenant. It was built with cedar boards, overlaid with pure gold, and fronted with gold chains. Its entrance had olive-wood doors carved with cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers and overlaid with gold.

l: cherubim (inner sanctuary), The First Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: Solomon made two cherubim of olive wood for the inner sanctuary, each ten cubits high, with wings of five cubits each, ten cubits from tip to tip, and of one measure and form. Their outstretched wings touched the two walls and each other in the middle of the house, and they were overlaid with gold.

l: gold, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: Gold was used to overlay the whole house within, including the inner sanctuary in pure gold, the altar belonging to the inner sanctuary, the floor, and the cherubim. Solomon also drew chains of gold before the inner sanctuary and overlaid the carved doors with gold fitted on the engraved work.

l: cedar, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: Cedar was used for the beams and planks covering the house, the timbers on which the side-room floors rested, and the boards lining the walls from floor to ceiling. The interior cedar was carved with buds and open flowers so that no stone was visible. Cedar was also used for the back part of the house forming the inner sanctuary, for the altar's covering, and for a course of beams in the inner court.

l: construction of the temple, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 6
s: The building began in the fourth year of Solomon's reign, in the month Ziv, 480 years after Israel left Egypt. Stone was prepared at the quarry so no hammer, ax, or iron tool was heard at the house during construction. The work was finished throughout in the month Bul of the eleventh year, taking seven years.

l: The First Book of Kings, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: Chapter 7 describes Solomon's thirteen-year construction of his own house, including the House of the Forest of Lebanon, the hall of pillars, the porch of judgment, and a house for Pharaoh's daughter, all built of costly cut stone and cedar. Solomon then brings Hiram, a bronze worker from Tyre and son of a Naphtali widow, who makes the two pillars Jachin and Boaz, the molten sea on twelve oxen, ten bronze bases with ten basins, and the pots, shovels, and basins. The bronze is cast in the Jordan plain between Succoth and Zarethan and left unweighed because there was so much of it. Solomon also makes the gold furnishings of the LORD's house, including the altar, the table, lamp stands, and hinges. He finishes the work and places the items David his father had dedicated in the treasuries.

l: Solomon, The First Book of Kings, Chapter 7
s: Solomon spent thirteen years building his own house, including the House of the Forest of Lebanon, the porch of judgment, and a house for Pharaoh's daughter, whom he had taken as wife. He sent for Hiram of Tyre, had the bronze vessels cast in the Jordan plain, and left them unweighed because there were so many. He made the gold furnishings of the LORD's house and put the silver, gold, and vessels that David his father had dedicated into its treasuries.
